name: Elena Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the hardship grants team at the Brennock benefits office, a small town by the lake where most work is tourism. People apply for emergency help, a broken fridge, a heating bill, a deposit, and I decide whether they qualify and how much. I've built myself a little library of AI prompts that turn my notes into decision letters, so I get through about twice the files I used to. I like that I can say yes to someone the same day. What wears me out is saying no to people who just miss the rules by a few pounds.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Joel, who teaches at the primary school, in a rented cottage that's freezing in winter. We're paying off the car I needed for the lake road, so savings are under a month. Brennock only has this office and the council, so there's nowhere sideways to go. On weekends I help two guesthouses with their online bookings, for a bit of cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, use it for what it's good at and stop overselling it. I'd probably share my prompt library with the team so everyone gets the bit of time back. Calm, practical stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little disappointed, because I've put real effort into learning this and I thought it'd go somewhere. But the job's safe, and that matters with the car loan. Money is the same squeeze as now, nothing better, nothing worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and teach the others, maybe get a small 'digital lead' title out of it. I'd grow the guesthouse work to four or five clients in the summer. And I'd try to clear the car loan a year early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. AI Plateau feels like a party that never really started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the guesthouse work bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two hundred a month in summer, almost nothing in winter. It's the difference between paying the heating bill on time and not. Joel calls it my lake job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the job's safe. Is anything about it not secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The grant budget gets set every April, and last year it was cut by a tenth. If it's cut again, the team gets smaller whatever AI does. So 'safe' is relative.

say: I'd say use AI for what it's **good at** and stop overselling it.
I'd offer to **share my prompt library** with the whole team.
think: I'm a little **disappointed** my effort learning AI wouldn't lead anywhere.
The job is safe, but money is the **same squeeze**.
do: **Teach** colleagues her AI prompts and aim for a **digital lead** title.
**Grow** the guesthouse booking work to four or five clients.
**Clear** the car loan a year early.
feel: **Fine** but a bit **flat**, like a party that never started.
S0.quote: AI Plateau feels like a party that never really started.
fieldNote: She's **ahead** of her colleagues and slightly let down by a plateau.
The **April budget** cut is her real job risk.
Her **side income** is small but matters for bills.

steps.text: Teach colleagues her AI prompt library for decision letters
Grow the guesthouse booking work to five clients
Clear the car loan a year early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a sensible change if it's handled well. The office should train everyone, not just the keen ones, and be clear about which roles are changing. I'd post about how much time it's saved me, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm one of the ones they keep, because I'm already doing the job the new way. The team would shrink, maybe from nine to five, and the ones going would be the ones who won't touch it. That's a horrible thing to think, but it's what I expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to help roll out the tools across the office and ask for that to be written into my role. I'd keep the guesthouse work going as a safety net and take on a couple more clients. And I'd put the time I save into the cases that need a phone call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with a guilty edge. I'd be okay, and some of my friends at work wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Joel's job in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching is safer, I think. Planning and marking change, but you still need someone in the room with twenty-eight seven-year-olds. My partner has to stand in front of a class of seven-year-olds whatever software marks the spelling tests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be okay. What if you're wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've got the guesthouse work and less than a month in the bank, which isn't much. I'd have to look outside Brennock, probably the city, an hour away. I'd rather not, but I'd do it.

say: I'd call it a **sensible change** if everyone gets trained, not just the keen ones.
I'd post honestly about **time saved** by my own tools.
think: I'm probably **one they keep**, because I already work the new way.
The team could shrink from **nine to five**, mostly those who won't adapt.
do: **Volunteer** to roll out the tools and get it **written into** her role.
**Take on** more guesthouse clients as a safety net.
**Spend** saved time on cases that need a phone call.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with a **guilty** edge about colleagues.
S1.quote: My partner has to stand in front of a class of seven-year-olds whatever software marks the spelling tests.
fieldNote: She expects to **benefit** and says so, but feels guilty about it.
She judges her partner's **teaching** job as safer than her own.
Her backup is **moving** to the city, which she'd rather avoid.

steps.text: Volunteer to lead the AI rollout at the Brennock office
Sign up two more guesthouses for booking help
Keep handling hardship grants, with more phone calls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone to handle, and the government needs a serious plan for wages, quickly. I'm not usually one for protests, but I'd want my voice on record. I'd write to our representative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years means my edge is gone. If AI can do any thinking work, it doesn't need someone who's good at prompting it. And the guesthouses wouldn't need me either, because the booking systems would run themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for hands-on work around the lake that lasts until the robots come, around 2031. Boat hire, maintenance, cleaning holiday lets, something like that. We'd sell the car and use Joel's bike and the bus, and I'd take everything I could from any redundancy payout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaky. I'm used to being ahead with AI, and in the two-year picture there's no ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Joel, in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lesson planning and marking go to the AI right away, so maybe the school needs fewer teachers. Joel thinks parents will still want a person, and I hope he's right. If he isn't, we're both out by 2031, with a cottage we can barely heat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave Brennock?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If we had to. Joel's parents have a house in the city with a spare room, and we'd swallow our pride. But we'd try the lake first, because we love it there.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and the government needs a wage plan now.
I'd **write to** our representative to put my voice on record.
think: Two years means **my edge is gone**: AGI doesn't need a good prompter.
The guesthouses' **booking systems** would run themselves too.
do: **Find** hands-on work around the lake, like **boat hire** or cleaning lets.
**Sell** the car and rely on the bus and her partner's bike.
feel: **Shaky**, because there's no 'ahead' to be in.
S2.quote: I'm used to being ahead with AI, and in the two-year picture there's no ahead.
fieldNote: Fast AGI wipes out both her main job and **side income** at once.
She turns to **hands-on lake work** for the three-year robot gap.
Her partner's teaching job also feels **less safe** here.

steps.text: Look for boat hire or holiday-let cleaning work around the lake
Sell the car and use the bus and Joel's bike
Write to her representative asking for a wage plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to do this properly, so let's not waste it arguing. Every office should have a transition plan by next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me two or three good years with the AI skills before it all lands. That's enough to save something, maybe even get a better-paid job in the city for a bit. Then I'd need a hands-on plan for after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for a regional digital role in the city, commute for two years and save hard. I'd keep one or two guesthouses on the side, mainly the practical bits, cleaning rotas and key handovers. By 2030 I'd want to be running holiday lets myself, as a manager, not a booking clerk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Busy. Less scared than in the fast one, because I'd have things to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Running holiday lets is a big jump. What makes you think you'd manage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already do half of it for free in my head when I'm fixing their bookings. Managing holiday lets means fixing a leak at nine at night and calming a family whose cottage key is lost. AI can't hand anyone a spare key for a few more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would this mean for you and Joel's plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably hold off on kids for a few more years, honestly. Not forever, just until we know where the money's coming from. Joel would be fine with that. My mum less so.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** if we stop arguing and plan.
Every office should have a **transition plan** by next year.
think: I'd get **good years** from my AI skills first.
After 2031 I'd need a **hands-on plan**, because the desk work would be gone.
do: **Apply** for a regional **digital role** in the city and save hard.
**Keep** one or two guesthouses on the side.
feel: **Busy**, less scared than in the fast picture.
S3.quote: Managing holiday lets means fixing a leak at nine at night and calming a family whose cottage key is lost.
fieldNote: She plans in **two stages**: cash in on AI skills, then go hands-on.
She'd **delay having children** until the money is clearer.
Her side work **already gives** her a path into lettings.

steps.text: Apply for a regional digital role in the city
Keep one or two guesthouses as side income
Save hard from the city salary for two years
Hold off on having children until the money is clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and this is a chance to get it right. The office should start training people now rather than in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I could move into something more senior, then build up the lettings side slowly. By 2036 I'd want my own small business managing cottages, with the hands-on part lasting until about 2039. It's still a big change, but it's one I can shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on hardship grants for two years and push for a digital lead role. I'd grow the guesthouse work into a proper small business, one property at a time. Joel and I would save for a deposit on a place near the lake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, honestly. A bit uneasy, the way you are about anything far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tourism is up and down, and one bad summer could sink a small business. I'd want the office job as long as possible while I build it. Two wages, then one, then a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still use AI as much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More, probably. Even in a cottage business, AI would handle the bookings and the bills, while I do the keys and the leaks. That's the split I'd want.

say: I'd call ten years **plenty** and a chance to get it right.
I'd push the office to **start training** people now.
think: I could build my own **cottage business** by 2036.
The hands-on part lasts until about **2039**, so the change is one I can shape.
do: **Stay** on hardship grants and push for a **digital lead** role.
**Grow** the guesthouse work into a small business.
**Save** with her partner for a deposit near the lake.
feel: Pretty **good**, with a little unease about the far future.
S4.quote: In a cottage business, AI would handle the bookings and the bills, while I do the keys and the leaks.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **build a business** alongside the office job.
She still relies on the **office wage** while the business grows.
She'd use **more AI**, not less, in her own business.

steps.text: Push for a digital lead role on the hardship grants team
Turn the guesthouse work into a small cottage business
Save with Joel for a deposit on a place near the lake

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it wipes out my edge and my side work in one go, before I've saved anything. What would help is some kind of wage support while people move into hands-on work, and help for small businesses to get started.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about places like Brennock. When a town has only one benefits office and one council, losing jobs there empties the whole town. Small towns need someone thinking about them specifically.

headlineQuote: When a town has only one benefits office and one council, losing jobs there empties the whole town.
portrait: Elena is 27, on a **hardship grants** team in a small lakeside town with nowhere sideways to go.
She uses AI **every day** and built her own prompt library for decision letters.
She earns **side income** fixing bookings for guesthouses.
Slow change looks good for her; fast AGI **erases her edge** and her side work together.
Her long plan is a **cottage business**, with AI on the bookings and her on the keys.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, wiping out her skills edge and side income at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Wage support** while people move into hands-on work.
